item.title: Martian Hadley circulation divides the atmosphere and connects the poles
Maximum earthquake magnitude unlikely to be controlled by subduction interface roughness
item.description:
Xiaodong Yang, Rebecca E. Bell, Alexander C. Whittaker, Haobo Xu, Xinze Han, Angela R. Knowlson, Valerie A. Locher
Nature Geoscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02093-z
Abstract Understanding the controls on seismogenic behaviour at the plate interface in subduction zones is essential to assessing the hazard they pose. The interface topography, or roughness, is widely thought to be an important factor, yet how roughness influences earthquake magnitude is still debated. This debate persists because, generally, studies are limited to individual subduction margins, proxies for roughness are used rather than direct measurements and historical earthquake records are short. Here we show by analysing data from 15 subduction zones globally that there is no relationship between any interface roughness parameter we derive from observations and a proxy for maximum earthquake magnitude. Specifically, for each margin, we use seismic reflection profiles of the plate boundary fault to quantify its roughness at 1–10 km scales, and in the same locations we test whether geodetically constrained interface coupling is an indicator of earthquake potential in lieu of a longer historical record. This analysis shows a strong positive relationship between earthquake magnitude and interface coupling, and that roughness parameters are unrelated to maximum magnitude or coupling. Our findings challenge the prevailing hypothesis that subduction interface roughness is a predominant control on its seismogenic behaviour and imply that interface roughness measured over length scales up to 10 km should not be used to assess a margin’s seismic hazard.

item.title: A strengthening yet less extreme Atlantic–European jet during winter
item.description:
Stefan Brönnimann, Yuri Brugnara, Patrick Kallabis
Nature Geoscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02069-z
Abstract The Atlantic–European jet stream is a key driver of weather extremes in Europe, yet its recent variability and trends remain poorly understood. Here we investigate daily changes in jet strength, tilt and latitudinal extent from 1725 to 2100 using pressure data from four European stations alongside climate model simulations. These indices explain about 40% of day-to-day temperature variability in Western Europe year-round. Weather extremes—including heat waves, cold spells, heavy precipitation and windstorms—are closely linked to the jet stream, and the indices also capture signals of sudden stratospheric warmings and major solar storms. Since the pre-industrial period, the jet has strengthened by 0.13 standard deviations and shifted poleward during the cold season. Future projections indicate continued strengthening in winter, while extremes in the indices become less frequent, suggesting a potential reduction in some types of weather extremes.

item.title: Experimental constraints on a long-lived magma layer at the Martian core–mantle boundary
item.description:
Rémy Pierru, Steeve Gréaux, Serena Dominijanni, Lianjie Man, Yoshio Kono, Sho Kakizawa, Yuji Higo, James Badro, et al.
Nature Geoscience
DOI: 10.1038/s41561-026-02104-z
Abstract Geophysical observations from the InSight mission suggest anomalously low seismic velocities near the Martian core–mantle boundary, possibly indicating a molten silicate layer. Such a layer would have major implications for the thermal and chemical evolution of Mars, but its origin remains poorly constrained because experimental data on iron-rich Martian melts at deep-mantle conditions remain scarce. Here we use in situ ultrasonic interferometry combined with X-ray imaging and diffraction to determine the melting phase relations, ultrasonic response and chemical compositions of co-existing melts and solids under conditions relevant to the Martian core–mantle boundary. Our experiments constrain a Martian mantle solidus about 100 K lower than previous estimates. We show that incipient melting rapidly weakens the elastic response, reducing wave speeds and modifying the ultrasonic signal character. Melts generated slightly above the solidus at 18–19 GPa, equivalent to a depth of approximately 1,550 km, are strongly enriched in iron (Fe# of 0.5) and reach densities comparable to or greater than surrounding solids, implying neutral to negative buoyancy. The combination of high melt density and low wetting angles favours the formation of an interconnected dense melt layer near the core–mantle boundary from a moderately FeO-rich Martian mantle without necessarily requiring overturn of an extremely Fe-enriched primordial reservoir and remains compatible with proposed thermal models.
